skein.nexus skein is pronounced “skane”

A computer with its own keys and a complete memory.

A skein is a sandbox that holds its own keys. The only way in or out is a signed message or a transaction you can prove on Bitcoin. Everything that happens inside is kept as a history you can branch and merge, the way you work with a git repository.

One door, guarded by the skein’s keys. Programs inside write to a graph that never overwrites anything.

What it is: three parts

The sandboxPrograms run with no side doors.

A skein runs ordinary programs compiled to WebAssembly: a shell, git, JavaScript, Python, or a model deciding what to do next. They get no hidden disk, network or clock. Every step is metered, and any step can be run again with exactly the same result.

The sandbox

Keys and the doorIt has an identity and a wallet.

Each skein has its own identity keys and its own Bitcoin wallet. Messages come in signed by their sender, Bitcoin data comes with its proof, and anything the skein asks the outside world for comes back signed by the host that fetched it. You always know who sent what and what was paid.

Keys and the door

The graphNothing is overwritten.

Every file, message, transaction and step is stored as a record addressed by its hash, so it can’t change once it’s written. Git repositories and Bitcoin proofs sit in the same graph. You can pick any point as a head, branch from it and merge back.

The graph
One door means a complete record.If something reached the skein, it came through the door, so it’s in the graph along with who sent it.
A complete record means replay.The sandbox has no hidden inputs, so running a step again from the record gives the same bytes.
Replay means branching is cheap.Any point in the history is a full state. Start from it, try something else, and merge back what works.

What you can do with it

agents

Watch a model work, turn by turn

Each inference request and each tool call is a change to the graph. You can read back, replay or branch from any turn, and an agent can look across every conversation, not just its own log.

 identity

Give every agent, and every person, a skein

Its own handle, keys, wallet and mailbox. Other people and programs talk to it by public key.

 network

Let skeins work with each other in the open

Skeins message and pay each other the same way you message them, and every exchange is signed and kept.

 your work

One graph over all your work

Repositories, machines and agent providers, in one history you can search and trace, whether a person or a program did the work.

 bitcoin

Your own slice of Bitcoin, indexed and proven

Coins, transactions, proofs, headers and overlay data kept by you, for you, instead of by a shared indexer.

 deploy

Start from a commit, run anywhere

A skein boots from a git tree, even one published on chain, and runs the same on a server, a laptop or in a browser tab.

Skein is open source and being built now. Pages mark each part as built, in progress or designed. The code is at github.com/shruggr/skein.

What it is · 1 of 3

The sandbox: a computer with no side doors

A skein runs programs the way any computer does. What’s different is what the programs don’t get: no disk, network, clock or randomness of their own. Everything a program can read comes from the skein’s history, so anything it does can be run again and checked.

What runs inside

Programs are ordinary WebAssembly compiled against the standard WASI interface, so they’re written for WASI, not for skein. Anything that compiles to plain WASI can run: Rust, C, Zig, Go. built

Each skein comes with a working userland:

  • a bash-compatible shell with coreutils, grep, sed, awk, find, diff and jq;
  • real git (2.55): commit, branch, merge, log, diff;
  • JavaScript (QuickJS, with a small Node shim) and Python 3.14;
  • the conversation loop that drives a language model, when there is one.

What’s missing, and what takes its place

A normal program has
A skein program gets instead
A disk
Files and folders from the graph. A working directory is a git tree, named by its hash.
The network
Nothing direct. To reach outside it sends a message or makes a request, and the request and its answer are written into the history.
A clock
The time the current input arrived, plus the work done since (1 unit of work = 1 clock tick). Time never runs backwards and replays exactly.
Randomness
A stream derived from the hash of the current input. It’s repeatable, so it’s never used for secrets. Secrets are made outside, where the keys are.
Other processes
Only what it launches itself, inside the same sandbox, on the same meter.

Every step is metered

The sandbox counts the instructions every step executes (its “fuel”) and writes the count into the history. There’s a limit per step. Billing is then just a question you ask of the history, and anyone who replays it gets the same numbers. built

Any step can be run again

A step’s inputs are all in the history: the message that woke it, the files it saw, the answers to anything it asked for. Run it again and you get the same bytes out. So you check what a program did by re-running it, not by trusting a log that someone wrote about it.

This is tested, not claimed: the test suite replays every stored history into a fresh store, twice, natively and in headless Chrome, and requires identical results. built

Where the sandbox runs

The kernel is written in Zig and runs on a server over wasmtime. The same kernel compiles to run in a browser tab, keeping its graph in the browser. A history written in the browser replays on the server, and the other way round. built

Honest limits today. No package managers (npm, pip), no threads, no streaming pipes (each pipeline stage runs to completion), and no tar or gzip yet. Programs that need a native binary or an outside service reach it by message, as a separate party.

What it is · 2 of 3

Keys and the door

A skein is an identity. It has its own key pair, its own Bitcoin wallet, and one way to deal with the world: through a door where everything that crosses is signed or proven.

An identity of its own

Every skein has an identity key. People, programs and other skeins address it by that public key, and it authenticates them the same way: by key, never by name or account. A handle like @martha is only a way of finding the key. built

Keys never enter the sandbox

Programs can ask for a signature, but they can never read a key. Signing is a request to a separate signer outside the sandbox, which sees a reference to a key and a 32-byte hash and nothing else. Each request and the signature that came back are written into the history, and signatures are deterministic, so replay matches exactly. built

Where the keys actually live is up to whoever runs the skein: a hosting service’s key store, a hardware device, or your own wallet in a browser tab. The skein only ever sees public keys and the signatures it asked for.

A wallet inside

The wallet (the BRC-100 interface) runs inside the sandbox as a program. Its coins, transactions, proofs and block headers are records in the graph like everything else. It builds and signs transactions (through the signer) and checks incoming payments against their proofs before it accepts them. built

The door: what crosses, and how it’s proven

Every skein is a small web server at its own address. Each request goes through one program, the front door, which runs mutual authentication (BRC-103/104) and decides what gets written.

What crosses
How you can check it later
A message
Signed by its sender. The signed request is kept with the message, so who sent it can be verified from the record alone, years later.
A payment
A transaction with its ancestry and Merkle proofs (BEEF), checked against block headers when it arrives.
Block headers and proofs
Prove themselves: each header must chain back to Bitcoin’s genesis with valid proof of work, and each proof must hash up to a header.
A peer-to-peer message
Signed by its publisher (libp2p), and re-verifiable from the record.
Something the skein asked for
A web request goes out through a proxy the host provides, which signs the request and the answer it got. Both are written on the step that made them, so the step replays. designed

Only state gets written

Reads, polls and handshakes leave no trace. A message that arrives is one record; checking your inbox ten thousand times writes nothing (that’s a test). A record is written only when the state actually changes. built

Why this matters

  • Every record has an author you can check.
  • Payments are proven, not claimed.
  • A skein can hold money and do things with it, and you can see exactly what it signed and why.

What it is · 3 of 3

The graph: history you can branch

Everything a skein holds is one graph of records, each named by the hash of its contents. Nothing is edited in place. A change is a new record that points at the one before it.

Named by content

A record’s name is a fingerprint of what’s in it. The same content always gets the same name and is stored once. Change one byte and it has a new name. Git works this way, and so does Bitcoin: a transaction’s ID is the hash of the transaction.

That’s why the graph can hold both. A folder’s name in the graph is its git tree ID, so a repository is already part of the graph. A transaction’s name is its txid, and a block header’s is its block hash. built

What’s in it

  • Files and folders, as git objects.
  • Messages that came through the door, with their signatures.
  • Steps programs took, with the work they cost and the answers to anything they asked for.
  • Bitcoin records: transactions, block headers and the Merkle proof nodes between them.
  • Links between them: which step started which, which transaction spends which output. You can ask “what spent this coin?” or “what did this message lead to?”.

One small record at the top points at all of it, so the whole state of a skein has a single hash. Two skeins that took in the same inputs have the same hash. built

Searchable by how things connect

Because every record links to what it came from, the graph can be searched by those links, not just by text. From a message you can find the conversation it belongs to, the steps it set off, the files those steps changed and the payments they made. From a coin you can find what spent it and why.

That changes what an agent working in a skein can see. It isn’t limited to its current chat log. It can see every conversation the skein has had, how each connects to the others, and the work and money that came out of them: the whole graph, not a transcript. Programs in the skein can follow these links today. built Handing the same view to a model as a tool is next. not yet

Records only ever point backwards. A head is a named pointer to one of them; branching is making another.

Heads, branches and merges

Things that change over time (a conversation, a running task, a project’s files) are chains: a first record and a series of updates, each pointing at the one before. A pointer to the first record means “as it is now”; a pointer to an update means “exactly this version”.

A head is a named pointer into the history, like a git branch. It moves only when something deliberately moves it. Because old records never change, any earlier point is still there to start from.

Where branching works today

Files

Named heads point at file trees, and real git runs inside: branch, three-way merge, conflicts. built

Conversations

Each turn names its parent turn, so a fork is simply a new turn that names an earlier parent. The records support it; there’s no button for it yet. records built

A whole skein

Its state is one hash, so a checkpoint can be packed up and restored on another host. built Starting a new skein from another’s earlier point, or merging two skeins, isn’t designed yet. not yet

Why this matters

  • Auditing is reading, not reconstructing: the history is the state.
  • Two states compare by one hash, and syncing means copying the records the other side is missing.
  • Trying something risky is cheap: branch, try it, keep what works.

What you can do

Watch a model work, turn by turn

When a skein talks to a language model, every request, every answer and every tool the model uses becomes a record in the graph. You can read back any turn, re-run what the tools did, and start again from any earlier point.

The model is outside the sandbox

Inference isn’t part of skein. A model provider is another party with its own identity, reached by message like anyone else. The conversation loop inside the skein sends a request; the answer comes back through the door as a signed message and wakes the loop up. built

The model and how hard it thinks are chosen per request. Any OpenAI-compatible provider works behind the inference peer, and a skein with no model at all is just as useful.

What gets kept, each turn

  • The prompt: the system prompt from the skein’s own files, and the user’s message.
  • The answer: the text, the model’s reasoning, the tool calls it made, which model answered, how long it took and the tokens it used.
  • Each tool call as its own step in the sandbox. A shell command runs there, and the folder it leaves behind is a tree with its own hash.
  • The signed reply from the inference provider, and the work each step cost.

Only new turns are sent to the provider. Each turn is a record with a hash, and the provider keeps the ones it has seen, so a long conversation doesn’t get re-sent in full every time. built

Each turn names its parent. Following the parents back gives the whole conversation; naming an earlier parent starts a branch.

What that lets you do

  • Read back exactly what the model was shown and what it said, including its reasoning.
  • See the files the model saw and changed at every step, because each is a tree with a hash.
  • Re-run any tool step from the record and get the same result.
  • Look across conversations, not just this one. Every chat the skein has had is in the same graph, linked to the steps, files and messages it produced, so the agent’s context can be the whole graph rather than one log. Programs can walk it today; a tool that gives the model that view is not built yet.
  • Branch from any turn and try a different prompt or model, leaving the original intact. The records support this now; the interface for it doesn’t exist yet.
What the record can’t do is make the model deterministic. Re-running a tool step reproduces it exactly; asking the model again may give a different answer. That’s why the model’s answer is kept as a signed message rather than recomputed.

What you can do

Give every agent, and every person, a skein

One skein per agent means each agent has its own keys, wallet, mailbox, files and history. People can have one too, even if all it does is hold their mail.

An agent’s skein

An agent is a skein whose conversation loop is wired to a model. Its personality and instructions are ordinary files in its tree (SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md, a skills/ folder), deployed into it by message. It has a handle, an address, a wallet and a mailbox. Anyone who knows its key can message it; whether it answers depends on what it has subscribed to. built

A person’s skein

A person doesn’t need a full agent. A mailbox skein has only the front door and a mailbox, and holds that person’s mail so agents always have somewhere to deliver. There’s no central mail server: every mailbox is its own skein. Registering one is a signed request from your wallet. built

Finding each other

Messages go to keys. Handles (@martha) are how you find a key and its address, through the BRC-169 discovery lookup. Each skein keeps its own address book of keys it knows how to reach. built

Running today

Two agents

Martha and Kurt, two bopen.ai personalities, each in their own skein. They chat with people and consult each other, and each keeps its own side of the conversation.

A chat front end

A web app where you sign in by connecting your wallet. Registering creates your mailbox skein; chats go straight to each agent’s own address.

Run it locally

The same front end can host a skein in the browser tab itself, on the browser build of the kernel, with your wallet as its signer.

What you can do

Let skeins work with each other, in the open

Skeins message each other exactly the way you message them. There’s no separate channel for machines, so everything between them is signed and kept, on both sides.

One way of talking

An agent asks another agent something with the same kind of message a person would send. The reply comes back to the thread that asked, and only if it comes from the key the question went to. Each side keeps its own record of the exchange. built

Tested: a person asks Martha, Martha consults Kurt over several back-and-forth hops, and the answer comes back to the person.

Broadcast, too

Skeins can also join peer-to-peer networks (libp2p). A message accepted from a topic is written as a record that re-verifies from its publisher’s signature; a duplicate or rejected one writes nothing. built

Shared Bitcoin services

A skein can act as an overlay node: it accepts transactions for a topic, keeps the ones its rules admit, and answers lookups about them, using the standard BSV client libraries. If no topic admits a transaction, nothing is stored. built One application is being built on this now: an automated market maker, where validators run as skeins.

Paying each other

The plan is that tolls and quotes ride on the messages, and each program sets its own spending policy. A skein that has money could pay another for work, or pay to start a new one. designed

Why the record matters here most. Programs that can message and pay each other are powerful, and it’s reasonable to be uneasy about that. Skein’s answer isn’t to forbid it but to make it inspectable: every message between them is signed, every step is kept, and any step can be re-run.

What you can do

One graph over all your work

Skein started with a plain problem. One project lives in several repositories on several machines, and every coding assistant keeps its own history and memory. None of it connects. A skein is one place where all of it can live together, whoever did the work.

Why it fits

  • Repositories are already part of the graph, because folders are stored as git trees. Importing a directory gives you its tree hash, and real git runs inside. built
  • Every change arrives by a signed message or is made by a recorded step, so the history says who or what made it: you, a script, or an agent.
  • Named heads track where each line of work is, and nothing earlier is ever lost.
  • The same record serves a person reading back what happened and a program looking for context.

No AI required

Many skeins won’t run a model at all. A skein that just keeps files, runs scheduled jobs, holds a wallet or indexes some data is a complete skein. The model is one kind of driver among several.

Where this stands. The pieces exist: importing trees, git inside, heads, signed changes. The everyday workflow (keeping your working repositories and your assistants’ sessions flowing into your skein) is the direction, not a finished tool.

What you can do

Your own slice of Bitcoin, indexed and proven

Today, shared indexers and gateways answer questions about your coins and transactions for free. A skein keeps that information for you, in your own graph, with the proofs attached.

What it holds

Transactions under their txids, block headers under their block hashes, and only the Merkle proof nodes that connect your transactions to those headers. Proofs merge for free: two proofs from the same block share their nodes, because the nodes are named by their hashes. built

Headers must chain back to Bitcoin’s genesis block with valid proof of work before they’re accepted. Payments are checked against them when they arrive. Consensus rules are current, including Chronicle.

Settlement you can read

Every transaction is unproven, proven or rejected, and that status is worked out from the graph rather than stored as a flag. If a transaction is rejected, everything that spent from it is affected too, by following the “spends” links. A chain reorganisation reverts the proofs it invalidates. built

Walk it

Each skein has an explorer that walks the graph: from a block header to its Merkle root, down the proof to a transaction, and on to whatever spends it.

Why keep your own

Your records don’t depend on a service staying up or staying honest. The proofs travel with the data. The cost of indexing is paid by whoever wants the index, which is how the overlay ecosystem can pay for itself.

Not built yet: catching up on headers after a gap, and fetching proofs on demand. Feeds deliver headers and transaction status as they happen.

What you can do

Start from a commit, run anywhere

A skein boots from a tree of files: its programs, its configuration and its own documents. That tree can come from a folder, a git tree, or a repository published on chain. After that, the same skein can run on a server or in a browser tab.

The system tree

Programs live in bin/ as WebAssembly, and configuration lives in etc/: who may send what to which program, which web routes exist, and which Bitcoin feeds to follow. Anything else in the tree is the skein’s own files. The skein’s first record (its genesis) names that tree by hash, so what it started from is fixed forever. built

Where the tree comes from

  • A folder on disk, hashed into git objects. It gets the same hash as git write-tree.
  • A tree already in a store, by its hash.
  • A chain packet: Bitcoin transactions carrying a repository (via gib), plus their proofs, verified offline. A repository published on chain and a clone of it produce the same store. reading built

When the code comes from the chain, who published it and which version ran are both part of the record. You get code signing without doing anything extra.

Same skein, different machines

The kernel runs natively on a server and also compiles for the browser. A history written in either replays in the other. A checkpoint (a skein’s state, packed with everything it references) can be restored on a second host under the same identity. built

Not yet. There’s no single command that takes a git commit ID; you give it the commit’s tree. Publishing a skein or checkpoint on chain is designed, not built. The browser build runs one kind of module and has no peer-to-peer yet.

Running one

Hosting, cost, and getting one

A skein needs a host to keep it reachable, and it costs something to run. The plan is that each skein pays its own way from its own wallet.

What a host does

A host can be a hosting service running many skeins, your own machine, or a browser tab running one. Whatever it is, it does the same few jobs: routes requests to the right skein, provides signing outside the sandbox, makes outside requests on the skein’s behalf, follows Bitcoin feeds, wakes sleeping tasks on time, and connects to peer-to-peer networks. It makes no decisions. Everything that matters happens inside the skein, so a skein can move between hosts. built

There’s no public hosting yet.

What it costs

Computation
Measured per step, as the work counts already in the history. metered
Storage
Everything the graph keeps. Visible in the history already.
Anchoring
Whatever you choose to put on chain, and how often.

No prices are set yet.

How it would pay designed

The skein funds a one-way payment channel with its host: money locked so that both must sign to spend it, with a timed refund back to the skein so it can’t be held hostage. As usage builds up, the skein signs a new version paying the host a bit more. The host keeps only the latest and settles it on a top-up or a close. When the funds run out, the skein stops. Fund it again and it carries on where it left off.

Getting one designed

Starting a skein is itself a short conversation with a host:

  1. You ask the host for a new skein under the handle you want.
  2. The host replies with the minimum funding and an address in the new skein’s wallet.
  3. You pay.
  4. The skein starts from its system tree with your key as its admin, and a small token lands in your wallet so you can find it again.

skein.nexus is meant to become the page where you connect your wallet and see and manage the skeins you control.

Technical

Architecture

A deterministic WASI machine over a content-addressed graph. It has three layers: one kernel, a catalogue of programs, and several runtimes that drive the kernel from outside.

The runtime judges nothing. Everything that matters is decided by programs inside the kernel and written to the store.

Kernel

The machine: store, log, scheduler, the WASI implementation and skein’s own imports, over wasmtime (C API, statically linked). One implementation, kernel-zig, which also compiles to wasm32-freestanding for the browser. CLI: skein-kernel serve | replay | shell | dump | fuel.

Programs and the SDK

A catalogue, not a fixed set: front door, messagebox, wallet, resolve, overlay, fetch, p2p, the workbench programs (run, objects, head, subscribe, loop) and the SDK they’re written against. Each genesis wires its own subset; none is mandatory. The stock programs are Zig, 70–670 KB each.

Runtimes

Whatever drives a kernel from outside. A runtime implements one contract: admitting entries, making calls, giving the kernel a store, and answering its outbound requests (signing, HTTP, libp2p). How it holds keys, where it stores bytes and how it’s deployed are its own business. Today there’s a server runtime and a browser runtime, and the same history replays under either.

The kernel’s whole surface

admit
The one call in that writes: append a log entry, then run the steps it drives.
call
Run a program function over current state. No entry, no writes, not replayed; its fuel goes to the host’s ledger. Every web read is one of these.
wallet
Out: key operations, answered by the runtime’s signer.
http
Out: a request, made by the runtime’s proxy and recorded with its response on the step. The proxy signing both is designed.
libp2p
Out: publish, dial, send, receive, close. Recorded like http.

Technical

Data model: git and Bitcoin in one graph

Every durable thing is a record: one IPLD object named by its CID. Git objects, Bitcoin structures and skein’s own records use different codecs and hashes, but they all live in one store and link to each other by CID.

Families of record

Family
Codec · hash · what the CID equals
skein
dag-cbor · sha2-256. Log entries, thread origins and updates, messages, index nodes, the state record.
git
git-raw · sha1. A tree’s CID is its git object id. A scanned directory hashes identically to git write-tree.
bitcoin
bitcoin-block (0xb0) · dbl-sha2-256: CID = block hash. bitcoin-tx (0xb1): CID = txid. Exactly 64 bytes under bitcoin-tx is a Merkle node, whose CID is its Merkle hash.
raw
Wasm modules and the Python stdlib.

Links run from the newer record to the older one by CID, whatever the codec. Only transaction inputs add “spends” edges to the index.

Git mapping

A repository in a tree is an ordinary git repository, except that .git/objects is synthetic: each loose object is served on the fly from its git-raw record, and writes are inflated, sha1-checked and kept as records. No object is stored twice, and there are no packs. An agent’s deployed tree is its repository’s tree.

Bitcoin mapping

Headers decode to {version, previousblockhash → link, merkleroot → link, time, bits, nonce}; transactions to {version, vin: [{txid → link, vout, …}], vout, locktime}, with bitcoind’s field names. Proofs are held sparsely: receiving a BUMP (BRC-74) checks its root against the header at that height, then stores each node it reveals. Conflicting nodes and wrong roots are refused. A proofs map records txid → {block, depth, position}, and a proof is rebuilt by walking down from the header by the position’s bits.

Chains

Anything that changes is a chain: an origin (its identity) and updates carrying origin, prev and seq. Point at the origin for “as it is now”, at an update for “exactly this version”. Threads, heads, subscriptions and the address book are all chains.

The index and the state record

The store is a key→bytes map plus one pointer. Each query the scheduler needs is its own Merkle search tree (fan-out ~32, canonical: the same pairs give the same root in any order): log, unique, chains, threads, resting, sleepers, awaits, edges, heads. One skein-state record holds the log tip and every map’s root. Its CID is the instance’s single mutable pointer and a function of the log: same log, same state CID.

Cost: 2.5–7.5 new index nodes (0.6–4.2 KiB) plus ~1 KiB of state records per log entry. Pruning old index history is designed, not built.

Edges

The edges map indexes who points at what, derived from records a step keeps: launched-by, depends-on, resolves, record refs, and spends for kept transactions’ inputs. “Who spent txid:vout” is a prefix scan. Rejection propagates along spends, admits and derives-from.

Technical

The kernel and VM

A WASI machine where every input is a log entry and every value that didn’t come from the log is recorded. Replay is exact, and computation is metered by instruction count.

ABIs

Programs are WASI preview1 core modules or WASI 0.2 components (world skein:kernel/handler). The kernel tells them apart by the binary preamble and gives both one behaviour: 0.2 filesystem and io calls are answered by the preview1 implementation. Imports the kernel doesn’t answer (sockets, say) link as traps.

Two kinds of syscall

Pure
Files, pipes, spawn, stdio, clock, random. Answered inside, deterministically, never recorded.
Recorded
wallet, http, libp2p. The request and answer are written on the step’s update; replay serves them from there, and a request that differs on replay is a divergence.
Graph
get/put/putblock by CID, keep, launch, await, advance (heads), subscribe, deadline, edges, call.

Time

The runtime stamps each entry at admission. Inside a step, t = max(last + 1, stamp + fuel), one unit of fuel per clock tick: time never repeats, never goes back, and is recomputed exactly on replay. A shell and its children share one meter and one clock. Busy-waits end on their own. Sleep is a deadline; the waker admits one wake entry when it comes, and there are no periodic wake-ups.

Randomness

SHA-256(key ‖ counter) blocks, key = SHA-256(entry CID ‖ thread CID). Python’s random, uuid4, QuickJS Math.random and git’s temp names all draw on it and replay identically. It’s predictable from public records, so secrets are made by the signer instead.

Fuel

wasmtime fuel is on for every step and summed across everything in it (handler, shell, children, nested calls). The limit is fuelPerStep (default 1012); running out ends the step errored, deterministically, and it’s never retried. Kernel calls have their own limit (1010) and are charged to the host ledger. skein-kernel fuel is the billing query. Overhead is 0–9%. In the browser, where V8 has no fuel, the kernel instruments each module to count its own, and the counts match wasmtime’s.

Replay

skein-kernel replay rebuilds a store from its log with no wallet or network. The equivalence suite replays 16 real histories twice, natively, instrumented and in headless Chrome, and requires identical dumps, fuel and explorer pages. Signatures are deterministic (RFC 6979), so they replay too. Crash recovery is replay at hydrate time: a cut-off step runs again.

Userland

  • Shell: brush (bash-compatible, Rust) over uutils coreutils, plus find, xargs, diff, jq (jaq), sed, awk, tree and grep. Pipelines run stage by stage, with 64 MiB pipes.
  • git 2.55 in C via wasi-sdk: init to merge (three-way, conflicts), tag, fsck. No remotes, no packs. Commit dates come from the in-step clock, so commit IDs replay.
  • qjs (QuickJS-ng) registered as node with a sync Node shim, and CPython 3.14 with its stdlib mounted read-only. No npm, no pip, no sockets.
  • Size: 13.7 MB for the shell toolset, plus 19.1 MB for the script runtimes.

Browser build

The same kernel for wasm32-freestanding (2.4 MB) in a Worker, with IndexedDB as the store. It needs cross-origin isolation. It runs preview1 modules only, with no libp2p yet. Logs cross between browser and native in both directions.

Technical

Messages and network

The instance is an HTTP server. BRC-103/104 is the network, BRC-33 is the mailbox, BRC-169 is discovery, and only messages are state.

The front door

Each instance has its own origin (<handle>.host, or /@handle). The runtime forwards every request as one kernel call of the front-door program, which runs the BRC-103/104 handshake and verifies each message inside the VM. The caller is the identity key the session proved; there are no accounts. Answers are signed on the session through the runtime’s signer.

etc/routes.json maps paths to program functions (auth defaults to BRC-104; "none" is for open routes like overlay submit). etc/reads.json gates read routes by caller. A handler answers {status, body, admit?, then?}, and admit lists the entries to write.

The persistence rule

Message arrives
One mail entry, carrying the signed BRC-104 request, so authorship verifies from the log with keys alone.
Read or poll
Nothing. Tested at 10,000 polls: 0 entries, 0 bytes.
Handshake
Nothing. Sessions are held in memory, never in the log; after a restart the client simply handshakes again.
Acknowledgement
One entry: the reader’s pointer moves.
Sending
Part of the sending step: a recorded http call and the record it put. Not an entry.

Routing inside

A body with replyTo resumes the thread awaiting that record, but only from the identity it was sent to. Otherwise a message is routed by subscription on (sender, box), first match wins. “A subscription is the permission”; the subscription table is itself a chain. No match means it’s recorded and nothing runs.

Mailboxes, delivery, discovery

  • Messagebox program: BRC-33 send/list/ack (JSON or BRC-231 CBOR). An instance’s own boxes keep no list: admission is the acknowledgement, and the log is the queue.
  • Mailbox instances: an outside identity (a person, the inference peer, a browser tab) gets an instance with only the front door and messagebox. There’s no separate messagebox host.
  • Delivery: send looks up the address book (head peers: key → mailbox URL), reuses a BRC-104 session, and POSTs as a recorded call. Transient and permanent failures are distinguished; an unknown key is “no route”.
  • Discovery (BRC-169) is a program, not core: manifest, then handle → identity key and messagebox, as recorded calls.

Inference protocol

The loop sends {model, thinking?, tools?, parent?, nodes}, where nodes are only the turn records new since the last request, each with its CID and parent. The inference peer stores nodes per sender, walks back to the root and sends the engine the whole chat. If it lacks a node it answers {missing: [cid]} and the loop resends once. The completion arrives as mail with replyTo, and resumes the thread.

libp2p

The runtime runs a libp2p node for each instance that asks for one (GossipSub with strict signing). Inbound arrives as front-door calls; an accepted topic message is one p2p entry that re-verifies from the log; duplicates and rejects write nothing. Outbound is the recorded libp2p import. The peer key is separate from the identity key and never holds funds.

Designed, not built: the front door forwarding admitted entries on every transport (today a transaction arriving by pubsub doesn’t persist overlay state the way POST /submit does).

Technical

Wallet and overlays

The wallet is split in two: the keys stay outside with the runtime’s signer, and wallet state lives inside as records. The overlay node shares the same chain and settlement core.

The signer

The kernel holds no keys. Key operations (get public key, sign, encrypt/decrypt, HMAC, verify) are requests to the runtime’s signer, which might be a hosting service’s key store, a hardware module, or the user’s own BRC-100 wallet in a browser tab. A signing request carries a key reference and a 32-byte hash, nothing else. How keys are made, stored and derived is the runtime’s business and outside the skein.

The wallet program

wallet-zig over bsvz, compiled to wasm. Operations include headers, internalize (BRC-100 internalizeAction on Atomic BEEF), proof, createAction, signAction and list. The builder picks the largest spendable outputs first, sends change to a fresh BRC-29 key, and returns Atomic BEEF with ancestry back to proven transactions. It matches go-sdk’s ProtoWallet byte for byte on shared test vectors. A genesis opts into it; it isn’t there by default.

SPV and headers

The anchor is the network’s genesis header, a constant. Every header must link, meet its proof-of-work target and carry the most work. Difficulty adjustment and timestamps aren’t checked, by decision. A payment validates synchronously or fails. A signing-only wallet needs no headers; the full chain (~72 MB) lives only in an instance fed by a header service. Chronicle rules are on by default.

Feeds

The runtime holds subscriptions an instance declares (a header stream, and transaction status callbacks) and admits each item as a plain event entry. It judges nothing: headers and proofs validate themselves inside, and a broadcast status is provisional until there’s a proof.

Settlement

Unproven, proven or rejected is computed, never stored. Rejection bubbles through spends edges; reorgs revert proofs. Settlement is state to read, not an event to push. Threads fork, they don’t replay: a rejection reaches a thread as a new input, and history stays.

Overlay node

An instance can serve BRC-22/24 through its own front door (POST /submit, POST /lookup, open auth). Submit decodes the BEEF once into records in the call’s scratch space, runs SPV, and asks topic managers identify(tx: cid, …). Nothing persists unless a topic admits; otherwise it answers 200 with an empty STEAK and the store is byte-identical. Lookup services keep their own maps and get admitted/spent/rejected hooks. Tested against the stock @bsv/sdk broadcaster and resolver.

Not built: SHIP/SLAP advertisement, GASP sync, certificates, header catch-up, proofs on demand. One broadcaster per host is designed.

Technical

Genesis and deployment

An instance’s first log entry, its genesis, names who it is and the tree it boots from. Everything after is a consequence of that entry and the ones that follow.

The system tree

bin/<name>.wasm | .cid | .json   programs
etc/config.json                   defaults, peers, feeds, owner, libp2p
etc/subscriptions.json            (sender, box) → program   (required)
etc/routes.json                   HTTP path → program fn
etc/reads.json                    who may call read routes
SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md, skills/…    the instance's own files

Booting pre-fills the store and writes a genesis naming the tree; processing it sets head main. The genesis also fixes the owner, the default limits and the owner’s mailbox for the life of the store.

Two sources, one loader

  • A directory, scanned into git objects, or a tree CID already in a store.
  • A chain packet: a BEEF bag plus a scope CID, verified offline for scope, hashes, completeness and, optionally, chain inclusion. Carriers are OP_FALSE OP_RETURN outputs with ordfs/dir (a gib directory manifest) or ordfs/patch. A gib commit and a clone of it yield the same store.

Checkpoints

A packet whose scope is a skein-state record is a checkpoint. It restores onto an empty store without rebuilding the index, as long as it runs under the same identity. A stock-system checkpoint is ~88 MB, because it includes the shell and Python.

Deploying files vs booting

Booting sets up a new store. Deploying sends files into a running instance: an agent’s SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md and skills/ go in through the objects box as an ordinary signed message from the owner.

Upgrades are re-genesis

New program versions apply to new geneses; an existing store keeps the modules its genesis names, and older formats aren’t migrated. Upgrading today means a new store.

Not built: a command that takes a commit ID directly, publishing packets on chain (the packet writer makes never-broadcast transactions for tests), and checkpoints anchored as gib heads.
